title: APA § 553(b)(B): good cause and alternative rulemaking sequences
shortTitle: APA § 553(b)(B): good cause and alternative rulemaking sequences
summary: Good cause permits omission of notice and comment when an agency contemporaneously explains why it would be impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.
notes:
The agency must state its good-cause finding and brief reasons when it issues the rule; counsel cannot first invoke the exception during later litigation. The notes describe different appellate approaches to review of that finding. Time constraints, emergencies, and technical or predetermined changes can support the respective rationales, but classification is subject to review.

Direct final rulemaking conditions an anticipated uncontroversial rule on the absence of adverse comments and promises withdrawal if opposition appears. Interim final rulemaking gives a rule immediate effect while inviting later comments and possible revision. Those procedures have different justifications and consequences. The GAO figures in the reading concern its 2003–2010 sample and do not measure every guidance document.

Hickman and Thomson identify risks that an operative interim rule can harden agency commitment or discourage comments. The materials contrast categorical invalidation of a later rule, acceptance of a completed later notice-and-comment process, and the intermediate judicial open-mind test. Little Sisters rejects that additional procedural test for the final rule; it does not hold that every invocation of good cause for an interim rule is valid.
